report_llm.text: The 33-homer, 37-steal projection isn't the headline — the Statcast profile explaining how he gets there is. His 49.1% hard-hit rate and .362 xwOBA sit well above the median, and the .255 xBA running notably lower tells you the contact quality is coming from fewer, harder strikes rather than a high-volume spray approach. The 26.7% strikeout rate is real drag, and a 34.4% chase rate tells you why. What keeps the profile honest is the 11.4% walk rate, high enough to offset some of the swing-and-miss and prop up the .362 OBP in the projection. At 29.5 ft/s sprint speed he's a 96th-percentile runner, and that speed inflates the stolen-base line and turns some ordinary batted balls into hits the xBA doesn't fully capture. The whole thing hinges on whether that chase rate stabilizes: if pitchers keep expanding him successfully, the strikeouts climb and the walk rate can only carry so much weight.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .414 xwOBA with a 2.71 xERA on the same Statcast card is not a formatting error. The bat is built on a 16.9% barrel rate and 13.9% walk rate that hold the profile together even with a 30.1% whiff rate that would concern you on a lesser hitter, and on the mound a 98.1 mph fastball spinning at 2488 rpm produces 30.4% whiffs against barrels allowed at just 3.8%. The projection, .286/.392/.549 with 38 home runs across 692 plate appearances, is conservative against what the Statcast profile actually says he is, and the honest dependency is whether he recaptures a full pitching workload after his injury absence. If he pitches anything close to a full rotation role, the two-way conversation ends and you're just describing the best player in baseball.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The tension here is simple: 18.2% walk rate against a 32.5% strikeout rate, two numbers pulling hard in opposite directions from the same swing decisions. The contact is genuinely elite when it lands, 93.4 mph average exit velocity and an 18.0% barrel rate both sitting near the very top of the percentile distribution, which is why the xwOBA of .373 runs so far ahead of an xBA of .243. He makes loud, infrequent contact, walks at a rate that almost nobody matches, and the projection's .387 OBP follows directly from that combination. The whole profile hinges on whether that 32.5% strikeout rate plateaus or climbs, because if whiffs keep accumulating the batting average drags the floor down to a platoon-adjacent outcome, but if it stabilizes, 33 projected home runs with a .877 OPS looks like a first-division regular who gives Oakland something to actually build around.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a legitimately interesting puzzle: a 53.6% hard-hit rate at the 95th percentile, 92.3 mph average exit velocity, and yet the xSLG sits at .442 with a barrel rate of only 10.7%. He's hitting the ball hard constantly but not squaring it up at the rate you'd expect from that much contact quality, which is why the projection lands at 17 home runs across 713 plate appearances rather than the transcendent power figure his athleticism once promised. The .288 xBA says the hit tool works, and 37 projected steals confirm the 28.9 ft/s sprint speed still converts on the bases. The whole profile hinges on whether he can lift the ball with more consistency, because if the barrel rate stays at 10.7%, you're looking at a very good player rather than the one San Diego built around.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.20 ERA and 0.70 WHIP across 82.3 innings at AA is the kind of line that makes you check whether the level is right, and the translation says it is. Anderson's 12 walks against 119 strikeouts produce a K-BB% that translates to 21.4% in a league where the average starter sits at 13.5%, and his translated walk rate of 2.1 per nine lands more than a full walk below the MLB mean. The command is the spine of the profile: if it plays up in the majors the way it's played at AA, you're looking at a mid-rotation arm or better; if the stuff gets exposed against better hitters and the walks climb toward league average, you're left with a multi-inning arm who misses enough bats to stick. One to two years out, with this much control at this age, the floor alone is worth something.

reports.published_report: The gap between a 96th-percentile xBA and a 3.8% walk rate is the whole tension in this profile. Harris makes extraordinary contact when he stays in the zone, and his .502 xSLG says the power translates, but a 44.8% chase rate is one of the worst in the sport, and it keeps the on-base number pinned near his batting average. The projection lands him at .285/.315/.484, which is a legitimate everyday impact bat if the contact quality keeps bailing him out of the plate discipline hole, and the 97th-percentile OAA rounds out a profile that earns its keep on both sides of the ball. reports.name: Ronald Acuña Jr.

reports.name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact grades are loud: a .291 xBA sitting at the 95th percentile, a 13.0% strikeout rate that very few hitters in the league can match. What the Statcast profile reveals, though, is that the bat-to-ball magic isn't translating into the thump it once promised — a 6.9% barrel rate and an xSLG of .413 that grades out around the middle of the league tell you the hard contact is there without the lift or violence to turn it into home runs. ValuCast projects 15 home runs over 664 plate appearances, and that number is the uncomfortable truth: elite contact skills housed in a profile that no longer generates plus power. If the barrel rate climbs and the launch angle cooperates, the .355 OBP floor plus sudden pop becomes a middle-of-the-order force again; if it doesn't, he's a high-average, low-slug first baseman who puts up a very pretty batting average and not much else.

reports.name: Josh Jung
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here has one legitimate wrinkle: a 91st-percentile xBA sitting alongside a barrel rate of just 6.3%. What that pairing says is a hitter who makes consistent hard contact, 48.3% hard-hit rate, but doesn't elevate enough to turn it into power with any frequency. The 18.4% whiff rate is genuinely clean, and a 17.9% strikeout rate means he stays on base without leaking outs — the projection's .284/.348 follows naturally from that contact quality. Where it gets complicated is the .435 SLG in the projection against a .432 xSLG from Statcast: there's no hidden power waiting to emerge, so the profile hinges on whether he can sustain that contact quality over a full season coming off injury. If he does, he's a solid everyday third baseman who hits for average, controls the zone, and doesn't hurt you; if the contact rate slips even modestly, the modest barrel rate has nowhere to hide.

reports.name: José Caballero
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost entirely bottom-of-the-barrel contact quality: 83.6 mph average exit velocity at the 1st percentile, a 24.3% hard-hit rate that sits near the very bottom of the league, and an xwOBA of .269 that ranks in the 3rd percentile. What keeps him employable is 28.1 ft/s sprint speed and a projected 40 stolen bases, which is genuine roster value even when the bat is this limited. The concern isn't whether he'll hit for average or power, he won't, it's whether a 5.3% walk rate and a 37.5% chase rate leave him with enough on-base value to stay in a lineup long enough to deploy the legs. At a projected .296 OBP across 487 plate appearances, he's a roster piece whose entire offensive contribution lives on the basepaths, and if playing time compresses or the stolen-base environment tightens, what's left is a glove-and-speed bench bat with a .662 OPS.

reports.name: Oneil Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact profile is genuinely split: 96.0 mph average exit velocity and a 16.7% barrel rate sitting at the very top of the sport, while a 37.8% whiff rate sits at the very bottom. That gap is the whole argument. The .358 xwOBA says he's generating elite damage when he connects, and a 10.6% walk rate keeps the on-base number functional enough that the projection lands at .340 OBP, but a 34.6% strikeout rate is a structural tax that won't quietly disappear. If the swing-and-miss holds at this level, you get a 20-homer, 29-steal fantasy asset who underperforms his raw tools; if he ever tightens the zone enough to trim that whiff rate materially, the .490 xSLG starts showing up in actual production and you have a star.

reports.name: Sandy Alcantara
reports.published_report: The fastball sitting at 97.5 mph is doing most of the heavy lifting, and it buys him everything else: a 5.6% barrel rate, a 6.2% walk rate that puts him well above most starters in zone discipline, and 211.2 projected innings at a time when durable starters are genuinely scarce. What he isn't is a swing-and-miss pitcher — 18.4% strikeouts and a 21.9% whiff rate are both below the midpoint for starting pitchers, which means his margin for error lives entirely in contact management and zone control. The xERA of 3.77 is honest about what he is: a volume-and-suppression arm whose value comes from accumulating quality starts rather than punching out lineups. If the fastball ticks down and the barrels creep up, the strikeout floor has nowhere to fall back on.

reports.name: Sam Antonacci
reports.published_report: The contact grades out as legitimately elite — a 14.7% whiff rate and 22.6% chase rate that together explain why his xBA sits at .286, but the power underneath it is limited enough to keep the ceiling honest. An 87.8 mph average exit velocity and 36.2% hard-hit rate are both well below average, so the .421 xSLG is doing more work than the raw contact quality earns on its own, likely propped up by batted-ball shape or luck in the current sample. reports.name: Ben Hess
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate translates almost exactly to MLB average, and the walk rate is the whole problem. At AA this year across 45.7 innings, Hess is running a 10.8 K/9 and 4.7 BB/9, and when you push those numbers through the level adjustment, the K/9 lands at 8.7 while the BB/9 bloats to 4.2, nearly a full run above what MLB starters typically allow. His K-BB% of 15% at AA translates to 12.3% at the MLB level, short of where you need to be to miss bats and avoid damage at the same time. The ceiling here is a multi-inning or setup role, and he gets there if the walk rate compresses enough to let the strikeout stuff play; if it doesn't, he's depth.

If he limits barrels more consistently, the 3.89 ERA projection becomes credible; if that contact quality stays where it is, the 4.37 xERA is the truer number, and he's a back-end starter earning his spot rather than a reliable arm for a pennant-race rotation.

What the Statcast card actually shows is a contact-over-power hitter: his 17.4% strikeout rate grades well and his 27.2% chase rate is disciplined enough, but a 34.8% hard-hit rate and 6.6% barrel rate mean he's not hurting you when he makes contact. The .320 xwOBA landing at the 49th percentile with a .265 xBA at the 73rd tells the real story, he's making weak contact at a survivable rate, not squaring balls up. A .300 OBP projection with a 6.4% walk rate is the ceiling of his plate patience, and if that speed ever erodes, what's left is a fringe bench outfielder hitting .238 with 11 home runs.

reports.name: Kaelen Culpepper
reports.published_report: The plate discipline translates cleanly: a strikeout rate that comes in below the MLB mean at 20.8%, and a walk rate at 9.7% against a game where 8.5% is par. Culpepper is doing the contact-and-patience things right at AAA, with 14 home runs and 16 stolen bases across 324 plate appearances giving the profile real two-way utility. The ISO translates to .157, roughly matching the MLB average of .15, so the power isn't carrying the ceiling here, the discipline is. Everything hinges on whether that contact quality holds against big-league velocity, because without it, the .263/.361/.464 AAA line compresses into a bench profile pretty quickly, and that's the ceiling anyway: a useful bench or platoon bat, with a floor that doesn't ask for much more.

reports.name: Lazaro Montes
reports.published_report: The power is loud enough that you can't dismiss the profile outright: 28 home runs across AAA & AA in 429 plate appearances, with an ISO of .294 that translates to .202 at the MLB level. But the strikeout rate is the whole argument against him — 31% in the minors becomes 30.8% in translation, and that's a heavy tax on everything else he does at 21 years old. The walk rate is genuinely good, 64 free passes in 429 plate appearances translating to 11.7% against an MLB average of 8.5%, which keeps his OBP afloat despite a .238 average against a .284 BABIP, but a left-handed bat who strikes out nearly a third of the time and can't make enough contact to run a higher average is profile-capped in most lineup configurations. If the contact rate doesn't move, he's a bench or platoon bat with real pop, and the floor is organizational depth.

reports.name: Kyle Harrison
reports.published_report: The 29.6 K% is the engine here, and the 5.9 BB% is what makes it work. Harrison's strikeout rate sits well above the league median while he's walking fewer than six hitters per hundred, and the 3.18 xERA says the run-prevention is earned, not borrowed from sequencing luck. The profile hinges on that command holding, because the 95.0 mph fastball isn't going to overpower anyone on its own, and a walk rate that creeps up would expose a hard-hit suppression profile that's closer to average than elite. If the command stays, he's a legitimate mid-rotation starter; if it slips, he becomes a high-strikeout arm living dangerously on the edges.

That contact profile is what makes the rest of the line believable: .313/.373/.548 at AAA with 11 home runs and an ISO of .235 that translates to .171 in the majors, above the MLB mean. The ceiling here is an everyday third baseman whose walk rate, currently 8% at AAA translating to 7.6% in the majors, needs to grow for him to hold a lineup spot against quality arms rather than filling out a DH platoon. If the bat-to-ball skill holds at the big-league level, he's a legitimate regular; if the contact rate softens under elite velocity and he doesn't draw more walks, you're looking at a second-division corner bat.

reports.name: Foster Griffin
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile tells you exactly who he is: a low-velocity, low-stuff pitcher who survives almost entirely on command, and the walk rate is the one number that makes the whole thing credible. His 5.7 BB% sits at the 90th percentile among starters, and that's doing real work against a fastball that lives at 91.5 mph with 2094 rpm of spin, both near the bottom of the league. His K% at 22.1% and whiff rate at 24.4% are both comfortably below average, so he's not missing bats; he's making hitters chase at 33.1% and then putting soft contact in play, which the 87.9 mph average exit velocity supports. The xERA of 4.07 is the honest read on the underlying stuff, so the ValuCast projection of a 3.28 ERA over 185.1 innings hinges entirely on whether that control stays elite — the margin for any command drift is essentially zero.

Across AA & A+, Doughty has issued just 17 walks in 82.4 innings, a 1.9 BB/9 that translates to 2.6 at the MLB level while most pitchers are surrendering 3.2, and the strikeouts are sufficient, 100 across AA & A+, without being the headline. The 24% K-BB% is the number that earns the trust, because control this clean at his age typically survives a level jump even when stuff doesn't sharpen. reports.name: Zebby Matthews
reports.published_report: The barrel rate is the problem. At 12.4%, Matthews sits at the 4th percentile, and the Statcast profile is honest about why: a 22.6% whiff rate and 28.2% chase rate that both land around the bottom quarter of the league mean he's not missing bats often enough to survive contact this hard. The 95.2 mph fastball keeps him from being simply overmatched, and his 7.6% walk rate is genuinely cleaner than most arms at this level of results, but control that doesn't pair with swing-and-miss is just batting practice with better location. The projection's 4.88 ERA over 119.2 innings reads as a back-of-the-rotation innings-eater, and the xERA of 4.64 says the run prevention isn't even unlucky — it's about what he actually is right now. The question this profile hinges on is whether he can develop a second weapon that generates more whiffs, because without that, the barrel suppression isn't coming and the walk rate advantage gets eaten alive.

reports.name: Nathan Flewelling
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of heavy lifting here. At 16% through 396 plate appearances at A+, Flewelling is drawing 63 walks against 106 strikeouts, and that discipline translates to an 11.5% MLB-equivalent walk rate that clears the 8.5% MLB average by a meaningful margin. The power translation lands right at the MLB-average ISO of .15, which tells you the .22 ISO at A+ is working against softer arms rather than carrying upward. The 27% strikeout rate is the load-bearing concern: it translates to 29.6% against MLB pitching, and a catching prospect who strikes out that often without a power premium above league average is a profile that hinges entirely on whether the walk rate survives the climb. If it does, you get a low-end regular with enough on-base value to matter; if the strikeouts widen as competition sharpens and the walks don't hold, what's left is a bench receiver who gets on base just enough to keep a roster spot.

reports.name: Nasim Nuñez
reports.published_report: The 52 projected steals are doing a lot of carrying here, because almost nothing else in the contact profile holds up. An 84.5 mph average exit velocity and a 0.4% barrel rate sit at the bottom of the Statcast leaderboards, and the xSLG of .276 confirms there's essentially no thump behind those grounders and rollers. What saves him from being a pure profile curiosity is the discipline: a 10.6% walk rate and a 25.8% chase rate suggest he knows the zone well enough to keep reaching base at a .320 clip even when the batted-ball shape is this weak. If the speed translates to bases at the projected rate and the walks hold, he's a viable second-division regular who manufactures runs the old-fashioned way; if the legs cool or pitchers tighten the zone on him, a .610 OPS middle infielder with no power is a bench piece, full stop.

reports.name: Justin Gonzales
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of heavy lifting here. At 14% in A+, Gonzales is drawing 51 walks in 369 plate appearances, and that discipline translates to a 10.3% MLB-equivalent BB% against a backdrop where most hitters sit at 8.5%, which is the part of his profile that survives the level jump cleanly. The power is a different story: 15 home runs and a .189 ISO at A+ look encouraging, but the MLB-equivalent ISO comes out at .136, notably softer than the MLB average of .150, meaning the bat speed or lift that reads loud in the High-A park probably doesn't carry all the way. The whole outcome hinges on whether the hit tool firms up at higher levels: if it does, he becomes an everyday right fielder who earns at-bats by getting on base; if the power stays fringe and the average erodes, what's left is a bench bat with a good eye and not much else.

reports.name: Gage Jump
reports.published_report: The fastball jumps off the card: 96.3 mph with 2358 rpm spin, both sitting comfortably above the median for starting pitchers. That combination is why the barrel rate is just 5.8% and the 25.5% strikeout rate is there to back it up. The problem is the 9.4% walk rate, which drags the xERA and xwOBA right back to league-average territory at 4.10 and .313, and keeps the projection ceiling at 115.2 innings and a 4.12 ERA rather than anything that announces itself. If he finds the zone more consistently, the fastball profile gives him a real shot at a middle-rotation outcome; if the walks stay, he's a back-end arm burning through pitch counts and earning quality starts eight times a year.

reports.name: Coby Mayo
reports.published_report: The contact problem isn't subtle — a 32.1% whiff rate and 33.5% strikeout rate that both sit near the bottom of the league tell you exactly where the ceiling lives. What makes Mayo worth watching anyway is that the raw power is genuinely elite: 92.7 mph average exit velocity at the 93rd percentile and a 50.3% hard-hit rate mean when he connects, he connects hard, and the projection's 19 home runs across 396 PA reflect that. The xBA of .215 explains the .208 projected average; he isn't getting unlucky, he just misses too often for the bat to stay in the lineup at a corner spot where you need more. If the strikeout rate ever bends toward league average, there's a genuine power bat here; if it doesn't, he's a platoon piece whose counting stats depend almost entirely on how often Baltimore runs him out anyway.

reports.name: Yandy Díaz
reports.published_report: A 14.4% whiff rate at 34 years old is the kind of contact skill that keeps a hitter useful well past when the rest of the profile starts to slip. Díaz makes hard contact at a 47.1% hard-hit rate, but his 7.0% barrel rate means he's spreading that contact around rather than elevating it into gaps and seats, which is why his xSLG of .440 sits modestly below his xBA grade of .284. The projection of .298/.373/.461 is basically what he is: a high-average, solid-OBP first baseman and DH whose power upside is capped by approach rather than bat speed. Hitters are making contact, just soft contact, and that's a sustainable skill if the stuff generating it holds. The puzzle is that his Whiff% sits at 22.2% and his Chase% at 27.0%, both well below average, so he's not missing bats the conventional way; he's winning through contact management, which is a narrower margin for error than strikeout-heavy relievers carry. ValuCast projects 72.8 innings at a 3.40 ERA with 20 holds, a middle-relief workload that fits the profile: not a closer, but a dependable high-leverage piece as long as hitters don't solve the soft-contact formula with better in-season adjustments.

Sterlin Thompson isn't hitting for power — his translated ISO sits at .14, right at league average, so the ceiling here is a patient, on-base oriented corner outfielder, not a run producer. Everything hinges on whether that contact approach and zone discipline survive the jump; if the strikeout rate creeps and the walk rate normalizes, what's left is a bench bat, which is also the floor.

reports.name: Charles Davalan
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power combination at A+ is genuinely unusual: 11% strikeouts, .234 ISO, 17 home runs, 16 stolen bases across 402 plate appearances. Most hitters who run that kind of raw power ring up strikeouts to pay for it; Davalan has 44 all season. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his K% at 16.4, well below a league-average strikeout rate of 22.0, and his walk rate translates above average too, which is how a .291 average at A+ becomes a .405 OBP. The ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat, maybe a plus one if the contact holds against better velocity at higher levels, and the floor is depth — the whole profile hinges on whether that 11% strikeout rate survives the jump to Double-A and beyond, because the power is modest enough at the MLB level (.157 ISO translation, roughly league average) that a contact erosion would unwind most of what's interesting here.

reports.name: Mason Molina
reports.published_report: The K-BB% translates to 13.3% at the MLB level, nearly identical to the 13.5% MLB average, which is the whole tension here: the strikeouts are present, the walks aren't quite gone. Across AAA & AA this year, Mason Molina has fanned 102 batters in 83.3 innings, but his translated walk rate of 4.0 per nine runs meaningfully ahead of the 3.2 MLB average, and that gap is what keeps this profile from being a clear middle-relief fit. If it doesn't, the strikeouts become a curiosity attached to a walk rate that bullpen managers won't tolerate.

The strikeout rate translates similarly below average, leaving a K-BB% that doesn't give you anything to lean on. His 1.3 WHIP at AA plays better than you'd expect given those numbers, and a 4.5 ERA over a real sample isn't alarming on its own, but the underlying shape points toward a pitcher who stays on the fringes rather than one who grows into innings. The ceiling and floor land in the same place: depth arm, the kind of guy who fills a spot when something goes wrong on a roster, and whether that's his fate depends entirely on whether he finds a mechanism to cut those free passes, because there's nothing else in the profile to carry him if he doesn't.

reports.name: Luke Stevenson
reports.published_report: Seventy-four walks in 354 plate appearances at A+ is the whole argument, and it carries weight. Luke Stevenson's 21% walk rate translates to 14.0% at the MLB level, dwarfing the 8.5% MLB average, which means the on-base skill likely travels even if nothing else does. The problem is that 100 strikeouts in the same sample translates to 30.5% in MLB context, and the .239 ISO at A+ softens to .158, right at the MLB average and unremarkable for a catcher who needs some pop to justify the position. If the discipline holds and the strikeouts play down as he climbs, he's a low-end regular; if the contact doesn't sharpen, you're left with a bench piece who takes a lot of pitches.

reports.name: Milan Tolentino
reports.published_report: The ISO is the thing. At .212 in 349 AAA plate appearances, Tolentino's raw power translates to roughly .162 at the MLB level, just above league average, which is a meaningful number for a shortstop with 13 stolen bases. The discipline holds up too: 46 walks against 107 strikeouts produces a walk rate that translates to 10.8%, and the strikeout rate, while ugly at 31% in the minors, comes out to 29.1% against big-league arms. Everything here hinges on whether the contact improves enough to keep pitchers honest — a .246 average sitting at the 49th percentile of AAA hitters and a BABIP of .335 suggest the bat-to-ball isn't carrying its weight, and if that gap between the power and the strikeouts doesn't close, this is a bench bat with a nice tool and not much else.

reports.name: Chase Shores
reports.published_report: The K/9 and the walk rate are pulling in opposite directions, and right now the walks are winning. At A+ across 37 innings, Shores has struck out 44 while issuing 18 walks, a combination that translates to a BB/9 of 4.1 when leveled to MLB, and the 5.60 ERA reflects the predictable result. The strikeout shape is credible, the K-BB% at 16% grades well within the A+ pool, and an MLB-equivalent K/9 of 8.3 sits just under the MLB average of 8.6, suggesting the swing-and-miss isn't disappearing when you account for level. But if the control doesn't sharpen as he climbs, the strikeouts stop compensating and what's left is a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway.

reports.name: Jim Jarvis
reports.published_report:
The contact-first shortstop profile is the whole argument here, and the power is what keeps the ceiling in check. Jim Jarvis is hitting .313 at AAA with 46 walks against 55 strikeouts in 348 plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate at 18.9% in a league that runs 22.0%, his walk rate at 10.8% where the field sits at 8.5%. The 32 stolen bases are loud. But six home runs and a .148 ISO at AAA translate to .13 against MLB pitching, and nothing in the shape of this profile suggests that gap narrows.

If the bat-to-ball and speed carry over, he's a low-end everyday shortstop; if a big league defense solves him, he's a reserve.

reports.name: Isaac Lyon
reports.published_report: The walk rate is what makes this profile work, and what would unmake it. Across AA, A+, and A in 2026, Lyon is running a 2.8 BB/9 that translates to 3.2 at the MLB level, exactly matching the MLB average, which means the control edge he's leaning on right now is roughly a wash once the competition sharpens. The strikeout side is the honest problem: 8.4 K/9 in the minors becomes a 7.4 MLB-equivalent while the MLB average sits at 8.6, and without swing-and-miss to pair with the command, a 1.1 WHIP and 3.1 ERA across 84.3 innings looks more fragile than it reads. If the walk rate holds and the strikeouts nudge up as he faces better hitters, he's a back-end rotation piece; if the strikeouts stay where they are, what's left is a depth arm who has to be perfect to survive.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Ty Southisene
reports.published_report: Thirty-one stolen bases, zero home runs, and a 12% strikeout rate — that's Ty Southisene's whole argument. The contact and patience are genuine: 41 walks against only 37 strikeouts across A+ & A, an OBP of .430, and a translated K% of 17.7% where most MLB hitters sit at 22.0%. But the ISO is .067 across A+ & A, translating to .085 at the big-league level while the MLB mean sits at .150, and there's no sign in 314 plate appearances that power is coming. If the speed and on-base skills hold against better pitching, he's a useful table-setter with a real defensive home at short; if they don't, there's not enough bat to fall back on, and the ceiling stays organizational depth.

reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile.
